source.publication: 2025 MI-1040 Forms and Instructions (includes Form 4884 instructions)
source.section: PDF page 19 'Which Benefits are Taxable' (joint returns use the year of birth of the older spouse); PDF page 22 question 3 (key person is the older spouse); Form 4884 Section A (PDF page 20 'Recipients born before 1946', private up to 131,794 joint; PDF page 21 Line 16); Schedule 1 lines 14, 27, 28 (PDF pages 14, 17); MI-1040 lines 9a, 10, 13-17 (PDF page 10 Line 9a, Line 10, Line 17; PDF page 11 example: line 14 income subject to tax less line 15 exemptions = line 16 taxable income)

worked: Federal AGI = spouse 1 private pension 90,000.00 + spouse 1 IRA 20,000.00 + interest 25,000.00 + taxable Social Security 34,000.00 = 169,000.00. Federal taxable income = 169,000.00 - federal standard deduction (31,500 + 2 x 1,600 age 65 or older = 34,700.00) = 134,300.00; given, not tested; the federal senior deduction is ignored. Michigan: all the retirement income is the younger spouse's (born 1951), but the key person is the older spouse (born 1944), so Section A applies: private limit 131,794.00, private benefits 90,000.00 + 20,000.00 = 110,000.00, all subtracted (110,000.00) on Schedule 1 line 27. Line 14 Social Security 34,000.00. Line 28: 29,376 - 110,000.00 < 0, so 0.00 (interest stays taxed). Subtractions 144,000.00. Line 14 = 169,000.00 - 144,000.00 = 25,000.00; exemptions 11,600.00; line 16 = 13,400.00. MI-1040 line 17 tax = 13,400.00 x 0.0425 = 569.50. No credits; state income tax 569.50. (Using the younger spouse's 1951 birth year instead would cap the subtraction at 98,846.00 and give taxable income 24,554.00.)
